paras.en: Astranis builds advanced satellites for high orbits, expanding humanity’s reach into the solar system. Today Astranis satellites provide dedicated, secure networks to highly-sophisticated customers across the globe — large enterprises, sovereign governments, and the US military.

With multiple satellites now on orbit serving customers around the world, the company is servicing a backlog of more than $1 billion of commercial contracts. Astranis is the preferred satellite communications partner for buyers with stringent requirements for uptime, data security, network visibility, and customization.

Astranis has raised over $1.2 billion from some of the world’s best investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, BlackRock, Fidelity, Franklin Templeton, and Snowpoint, and employs a team of 500 engineers and entrepreneurs. Astranis designs, builds, and operates its satellites out of its 153,000 sq. ft. headquarters in Northern California, USA.

articles.title: Ukrainian startup, GomSpace test satellite for future communications network
articles.author: Sandra Erwin

paras.en: WASHINGTON — A Ukrainian defense technology company and a Danish satellite manufacturer have begun operating an experimental communications satellite in orbit.

Ukrainian startup Himera and Denmark’s GomSpace said Oct. 27 that their Obria Nano satellite, launched Oct. 1 aboard the SpaceX Transporter-18 rideshare mission, is undergoing tests. The companies plan to design a constellation that would provide communications coverage across Ukraine.

The project is one of at least two European-backed initiatives aimed at giving Ukraine greater control over satellite communications, following disruptions this month to SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield services that affected Ukrainian military operations.

The announcement comes five days after Finnish satellite manufacturer Iceye and telecommunications equipment maker Nokia signed a letter of intent with Ukraine’s Defense Ministry to explore developing a sovereign broadband satellite communications network.

Ukraine has relied heavily on SpaceX’s satellite services for battlefield communications since Russia’s invasion in 2022. The services have become essential to military command networks, drone operations and communications in areas where terrestrial infrastructure has been destroyed or disrupted.
But restrictions imposed in mid-October limited satellite connectivity, interfering with Ukrainian drone operations, including efforts to intercept Russian attack drones.

Ukraine said Oct. 24 that Starlink and Starshield services had returned to normal operating speeds. The disruptions prompted a dispute over responsibility, with SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and U.S. officials offering conflicting explanations about who had authorized the limits.

Himera and GomSpace said the Obria Nano project is intended to establish a communications system under Ukrainian control, with plans eventually to manufacture satellites and ground terminals domestically.

“For us, this project is about more than launching a satellite. It is an opportunity to lay the foundation for an independent communications network for Ukraine,” said Misha Rudominski, Himera’s co-founder and chief executive.

“We are starting by testing technologies in orbit, while our long-term goal is to develop capabilities that will strengthen the country’s strategic security and reduce dependence on external communications providers,” he said.
Himera, founded in 2022, develops secure tactical radio systems for military forces, including equipment designed to operate in environments affected by electronic warfare.
GomSpace, headquartered in Aalborg, Denmark, manufactures small satellites, communications payloads and spacecraft subsystems.

The companies said Obria Nano is operating in orbit and undergoing testing that will inform the design of a constellation. They did not disclose the satellite’s specifications, communications capacity, project financing or the number of satellites envisioned for the network.

Neither European initiative is expected to replace Starlink’s extensive global network. Smaller national constellations could provide dedicated communications for selected military operations while supplementing commercial services.

articles.title: NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon
articles.author: Lee Mohon

paras.en: In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.

Agency leadership provided updates on the previously announced acceleration plans for the Artemis program, advancing toward the agency’s Artemis III test flight in 2027 and Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028. Building on the priorities announced at Ignition earlier this year, NASA leadership shared the agency’s significant progress across its missions, working with industry partners to test critical capabilities, reduce risk, and build toward a sustained American presence on the Moon.

“This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible,” said Isaacman. “NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we’re not waiting for others to bring their plans to us — the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.”

The agency shared details of the Artemis III mission, which will test rendezvous, docking, and operations between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar lander test vehicles from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit. Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, launched on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission.

The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence: Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship.

The Oct. 23 updates follow other recent updates about the Artemis missions. Hardware for Artemis III is on track, with processing timelines sharply reduced by about half. NASA also redesigned, built, and tested a critical fuel-line component in-house in five months, at roughly a tenth of the cost of an earlier outside-vendor estimate.

“NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it,” said Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager. “It’s an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.”
Artemis IV: Pursuing multiple paths to Moon landing

For the agency’s Artemis IV mission in 2028, astronauts will launch aboard Orion on the SLS rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop lunar landers to carry those astronauts to the Moon’s surface. Both companies have redesigned their approaches to simplify the missions and make them more efficient and flexible as compared to previous mission designs.

SpaceX’s Starship will refuel in Earth orbit, rendezvous with Orion, and then carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Blue Origin’s approach involves transfer stages in Earth orbit to push its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander toward the Moon, where it will meet Orion in a closer lunar orbit before descending to the surface.
Both SpaceX and Blue Origin are targeting to be able to support a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

For Artemis IV, NASA is pursuing two upper-stage options for the SLS rocket: its current stage, the interim cryogenic propulsion stage; and a stretched version of ULA’s Centaur V which can carry more propellant. Pursuing both options ensures NASA is maintaining flexibility and preventing single-point dependency.

NASA also announced plans with spacesuit provider Axiom Space to develop a second, lighter suit design called the “Sortie suit” to enable the first moonwalks. The Sortie suit will not replace Axiom’s primary suit, which will be used for longer, more demanding missions in the future. The Sortie suit is roughly half the weight of the larger suit and lets NASA move faster on the earliest surface missions.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions at the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

articles.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
articles.author: Cheryl Warner

paras.en: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.

The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next. We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics. This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. “It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”

The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight.
With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.

articles.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites

paras.en: The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous, with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic crust. Over time, portions of this oceanic rock were wrenched upward by tectonic forces, eventually emerging as a rugged island made of ophiolite, a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake. Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of the Troodos Mountains.

During the Miocene, considerably younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl, and other marine sedimentary rocks accumulated around the island, providing material that developed into a second, smaller island to the south during a later period of geologic uplift. Over time, sediment poured from rivers into the channel separating the two islands and combined with marine sediments to create deltas and eventually two land bridges, or tombolos. The joined landmass comprises the Akrotiri Peninsula, now the southernmost tip of Cyprus.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The sandy edges of the peninsula were visible when Landsat 8 captured these images on October 10, 2026. Akrotiri Salt Lake, a coastal lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos. The more westerly feature, the Kouris River tombolo, formed first, developing about 50,000 years ago from river-deposited gravels and sands. The eastern tombolo extended southward from Cyprus, cutting off the Mediterranean Sea only within the past 2,000 years, according to geologists.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The lake's water levels now vary markedly with the seasons, typically filling in the late autumn and winter and drying out in the summer. The influx of winter water has historically attracted sizable overwintering flamingo populations, averaging about 4,000 birds. However, the wintering flamingo population has declined in recent years, plummeting to 30 birds in 2025, according to news reports. Flamingos have long flocked to the lake to feed on fairy shrimp, which are rich in colorful substances called carotenoids that give the birds their famously pink hue.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Snakes are another of the island's more notorious animal inhabitants. In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa, or "land of snakes," likely due to its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers. According to legend, the island's snake communities grew to be so problematic during a drought in the fourth century that the Roman Empress Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control the venomous reptiles.

The first feline imports were released in a particularly snake-infested area on the southeastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata (Cape Cat in Greek). The cape today is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats, a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes. Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more than one million of the feline predators stalking the island. The handful of nuns who now live in the monastery still care for hundreds of cats, according to the St. Nicholas Center.

articles.title: Gunfire damages tents at Rafah displacement site in Gaza, as aid teams prepare for winter storms

paras.en: Gunfire damages tents at Rafah displacement site in Gaza, as aid teams prepare for winter storms

Gunfire hit and damaged multiple tents at a displacement site in Gaza’s northern Rafah region on Tuesday, reportedly causing injuries and forcing a humanitarian partner to leave the area, the UN aid coordination office (OCHA) has said.
The NGO had been working on flood control ahead of the rainy season, OCHA added in the Wednesday update.
On the same day, small arms fire was reported near a UN-contracted facility in Deir al Balah and close to a UN-organized convoy in Rafah. No injuries to UN staff or damage were reported.
The incidents came amid continued reports of strikes hitting populated areas and causing civilian casualties across the Gaza Strip.

“Civilians, including humanitarian workers, must always be protected, and civilian objects, including humanitarian facilities and vehicles, must always be spared,” the Secretary-General’s Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told journalists.

Despite the insecurity, relief efforts continue. In the last week of October, the UN and its partners supported more than 70 households who lost their shelters and other belongings in incidents ranging from airstrikes to domestic fires.
During that same week, child protection partners reached nearly 4,500 boys and girls and more than 2,000 caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support.

They identified almost 200 children in need of individually tailored support, including 20 who are unaccompanied or separated from their families and 17 who are injured. Follow-up support continues for more than 2,000 children identified earlier as needing such help.
Partners also provided vouchers to buy autumn clothes for more than 1,000 children without parental care.
In the West Bank, the olive harvest continues to be disrupted by Israeli settler violence and restrictions on Palestinians’ access to their groves, according to OCHA.

Food security partners have provided harvesting tools and machinery across nearly 80 per cent of all identified hotspots, while protection partners have supported volunteer harvesting campaigns and a protective presence for Palestinian farmers.
In most locations, however, assistance can reach only a limited number of olive pickers due to funding shortfalls, violence and Israeli restrictions, OCHA said.

articles.title: UN peacekeeping chief warns of ‘security vacuum’ as Blue Helmets leave Lebanon and Western Sahara

paras.en: UN peacekeeping chief warns of ‘security vacuum’ as Blue Helmets leave Lebanon and Western Sahara

The UN’s peacekeeping chief warned on Wednesday that the withdrawal of “Blue Helmets” from Lebanon and Western Sahara risks leaving a dangerous security vacuum, while the Security Council remains divided over what, if anything, should replace them.

The UN mission in Western Sahara closed on 31 October after 35 years. In Lebanon, the peacekeeping force that has patrolled the border with Israel since 1978 is due to cease operations at the end of the year.
“What happens when there is no longer a third-party presence between the Lebanese army and the Israel Defense Forces?” asked Jean-Pierre Lacroix, Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations.

Briefing journalists at UN Headquarters in New York, Mr. Lacroix said the organization was losing some of its longest-standing military deployments, with no guarantee that the countries concerned could maintain stability on their own.

Around 7,500 peacekeepers are still serving with the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL). The force acts as a go-between for the Lebanese and Israeli armies, monitors violations and helps humanitarian aid get through.

Mr. Lacroix has just returned from Lebanon. He said President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam had told him they feared a “security vacuum” once the peacekeepers leave, with no one left to stop border incidents from turning into clashes.
He also raised questions over the future of the Blue Line, which the UN drew to mark Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanon in 2000.

There is a humanitarian cost too. Mr. Lacroix offered a cautious estimate that about 10,000 people are still living between the Blue Line and the forward defence line Israel has set up inside Lebanese territory. Their access to aid depends heavily on UNIFIL.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres put forward options in June, but the Security Council has yet to agree on any follow-on arrangement. Mr. Lacroix urged council members to decide what form a future international presence could take.

The same deadlock has already ended the UN’s presence in Western Sahara. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) shut down on 31 October after council members failed to agree on renewing its mandate.

Russia vetoed a United States draft that would have reshaped the mission around a solution based on autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty. A rival Russian text calling for a one-year renewal fell short of the nine votes needed to pass.

MINURSO was set up in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front. It never held the self-determination referendum it was created to organize, and hostilities in the territory resumed in 2020.

Mr. Lacroix confirmed that the mission was now in its liquidation phase. The UN is urging the parties to show restraint and remains committed to a political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara.

Mr. Lacroix also recently visited Syria and peacekeepers serving in the Golan. He said UN observers there were receiving complaints from civilians about detentions, movement restrictions and property seizures linked to the Israeli military presence. He said their mediation had led to several people being released and some property being returned.

In Abyei, the territory disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, recent drone attacks have highlighted another growing danger. Blue Helmets are having to adapt to technologies that put both their own personnel and the civilians they protect at risk.
The UN is reviewing its military and technological capabilities. But Mr. Lacroix said the answer could not be purely technical. Above all, he said, it was a matter of “political responsibility”.

articles.title: COP31 explained: What’s at stake at this year’s UN climate summit?

paras.en: COP31 explained: What’s at stake at this year’s UN climate summit?

The world has more tools than ever to tackle climate change, yet millions remain unable to benefit from them. As clean energy technologies advance faster than ever, the challenge facing countries at COP31 is no longer just finding solutions – but making sure everyone can afford them.

Catastrophic floods, deadly heatwaves and prolonged droughts have been a hallmark of 2026, a year in which scientists confirmed that the world is on track to exceed the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold.

Against this backdrop, and with a powerful El Niño expected to intensify climate impacts further, representatives of more than 190 countries will gather in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November for COP31, the latest iteration of the keynote annual UN climate conference.

While fossil fuels remain the main driver of warming emissions, the technologies needed to move away from them are advancing at an extraordinary pace. Solar power, electric vehicles and battery storage are becoming increasingly accessible.
Yet many countries continue to struggle to benefit from them. Why?

Ahead of the summit, UN News spoke with Selwin Hart, the UN Special Adviser on Climate Action and Just Transition, about what's at stake, what’s holding back progress and what another round of climate diplomacy can realistically achieve.

COP stands for Conference of the Parties, in this case, the countries that are parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). These annual gatherings allow governments to assess progress and negotiate how to tackle a challenge that no nation can solve alone.
The talks produced the landmark Paris Agreement in 2015, when countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
COPs now extend well beyond government negotiations. Businesses, scientists, Indigenous Peoples, young people and civil society increasingly participate, reflecting the scale of the challenge.
“There’s now a clear recognition that addressing the climate crisis requires all hands on deck,” Mr. Hart explains.
A COP is often judged by the agreement reached at the end, sometimes after days of difficult discussions and last-minute compromises. But Mr. Hart argues that this tells only part of the story.
He identifies three ways these conferences can make a difference:
- Negotiated agreements: Countries seek consensus on issues such as climate finance, emissions reductions and adaptation, though geopolitical divisions often make ambitious outcomes difficult.

- The Action Agenda: Governments, development banks, businesses and civil society organizations work together on practical solutions, from expanding renewable energy and modernizing electricity networks to reducing methane emissions.
- National commitments: Countries use COPs to announce actions at home, including new climate plans, commitments to move away from fossil fuels and contributions to climate funds.
“There’s sometimes this expectation that COPs will always have this big grand deal that will solve the climate crisis. That’s not realistic,” Mr. Hart says.
There’s sometimes this expectation that COPs will always have this big grand deal that will solve the climate crisis. That’s not realistic
This year, Türkiye will host and preside, while Australia is leading the negotiations, working closely with Pacific Island countries.
The summit places particular emphasis on implementation, with Türkiye promoting initiatives on clean energy, food security, resilient cities, greener industries, oceans and waste reduction.
“I’m running a personal campaign to rename the Action Agenda, the Implementation Agenda,” says the top climate adviser, underscoring the need to move beyond promises and focus on practical solutions.
Behind the diplomatic language are decisions that could affect millions of lives. Several major issues remain unresolved:

- Climate finance: Developing countries want wealthier nations to fulfil their financial commitments under the Paris Agreement, while disagreements persist over funding responsibilities, access to finance and how global financial flows can be directed towards climate action.
- Just transition: Countries agreed last year to establish a mechanism to support the shift to cleaner economies – but still need to decide how it will work.
- Adaptation: Negotiators will continue to work on measuring progress while developing countries press for greater financial support.
- Cutting emissions: Governments remain divided over how to strengthen emissions action and deliver on existing commitments.
COP31 will also launch the second global stocktake, the Paris Agreement’s formal process for assessing collective progress towards its long-term goals.
But, haven’t we already lost the fight against global warming?

Scientists warn that the world is set to temporarily exceed the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold, a situation known as overshoot. But how far temperatures rise, and for how long, still depends on the choices governments, businesses and societies make today.

“Overshoot is not surrender. Overshoot should really lead to a much greater degree of urgency,” Mr Hart says, calling for faster emissions cuts and greater investment in protecting vulnerable communities.
Despite the warning, he sees reasons for optimism.

“The good news in this horrible situation of overshoot is that the world has never been better equipped to solve this challenge,” he says, pointing to the rapid expansion of electric vehicles, solar energy and battery storage.
Just a decade ago, the clean energy transition looked very different. The technological frontier is expanding at a remarkable pace.
- Electric vehicles: Ten years ago, fewer than one in 100 new cars sold worldwide was electric. In 2025, it was one in four, and that share is expected to reach 28 per cent in 2026.
- Solar power: The world added more than 600 gigawatts of solar power capacity in 2025, accounting for over three-quarters of new renewable power capacity.

- Battery storage: Global battery storage capacity is now 11 times higher than in 2021. In 2025 alone, the world added 108 GW – 40 per cent more than the previous year. These systems allow electricity generated by solar panels and wind turbines to be stored and used later
If the solutions exist, what’s holding us back?
Clean energy investment has grown rapidly, but its benefits have been far from equally distributed.
Emerging and developing economies outside China, home to nearly two-thirds of the world's population, received just 18 per cent of global clean energy investment in 2025.

Africa illustrates the challenge. Despite its enormous renewable energy potential, the continent attracts only a small share of global investment, while around 600 million people still lack access to electricity.

Mr. Hart says capital investment is one of the biggest obstacles. Financing renewable energy projects in developing countries can cost several times more than in wealthier nations, even when the technology is identical.
“So, our task now, in this second decade of the Paris Agreement, is to ensure that we remove the barriers to implementation, the barriers to faster action in these economies,” he explains.

For countries already struggling with heavy debt burdens, the challenge is particularly difficult, leaving governments with limited resources to invest in healthcare, education and climate protection.
“We need solutions on finance that will not increase debt,” Mr. Hart stresses.
COP31 will not solve the climate crisis in two weeks. But it could help remove some of the barriers standing between the solutions already available and the people who need them.
For millions living with the consequences of a warming planet, that is what will matter long after the summit ends.
Follow the latest developments from COP31 through our new podcast, Talk & Action, and our special daily coverage of the conference.

articles.title: 'Sloppy' Arsenal survive second-half scare to beat Slavia Prague

paras.en: Slavia Prague vs Arsenal; UEFA Champions League
Slavia Prague vs Arsenal. UEFA Champions League.
Slavia Prague 1-2 Arsenal: Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyokeres on target as Gunners survive second-half scare

Report as Arsenal move up to third in Champions League league phase table with 2-1 win over Slavia Prague; Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyokeres scored as the Gunners withstood second-half pressure to continue their unbeaten start in the competition
Arsenal survived a second-half fightback from Slavia Prague to win 2-1 at the Fortuna Arena and continue their unbeaten start to the season in the Champions League.
The Gunners, runners-up last term, appeared on course for an emphatic victory after scoring twice through Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyokeres in a one-sided first half.
But Slavia roared back into the contest in the second period and gave Arsenal a scare as Wiktor Nowak's late goal from close range set up a nervous finale for Mikel Arteta's side.
- As it happened | How the teams lined up | Match stats
- Champions League fixtures and results | Table | Latest: Arsenal

Arsenal hung on to claim their third win in four Champions League games but needed a goal-line clearance from Gabriel Magalhaes and several saves from David Raya, who brilliantly pushed an Oskar Kubiak header against the post shortly before Slavia's goal.
Slavia had 17 shots in the second half, having only had one before the break as Arsenal were made to work for a result which looked a foregone conclusion after their dominant start.
Arteta freshened up his side with six changes from Sunday's 1-0 win over Liverpool and Arsenal scored their early opener when Madueke finished coolly having been put through on goal by Gyokeres.
The striker added the second with a sumptuous, curling finish after combining with Mikel Merino but Arsenal missed chances to extend their lead before the break and Slavia responded.

A switch from a back four to a back three allowed the hosts to commit more bodies forward and they tested Arsenal's resolve with a succession of chances. Raya's goal was eventually breached but the win sees the Gunners move up to third in the league phase table.

Gyokeres didn't score a single goal in his first 10 appearances of the season for Arsenal but his brilliantly taken effort against Slavia Prague makes it two in his last three following his goal in the Carabao Cup tie against Fleetwood Town last week.

He will need to do it against stronger opposition if he is to prove he should usurp Kai Havertz as Arteta's first-choice No 9. But this was an encouraging display which suggests the Sweden international might be turning a corner after a tough start to the campaign.
His goal, immaculately dispatched into the far corner from the left-hand side of the box, will be his biggest source of satisfaction. But there were signs of improvement in his all-round game too.

Gyokeres created the opener with a smart pass around the corner for Madueke and had plenty of other bright moments with his back to goal, linking the play tidily, bringing others to play, and ultimately making an invaluable contribution to a hard-fought victory.
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta to TNT Sports:
"Obviously we need to value that winning away in the Champions League is extremely difficult. We knew that - and we knew the players and the opponent that we had in front of us.
"Two very different halves, the first one we played a really high level - exceptional at times, I would say. The scoreline should have reflected three or four goals. We didn't do it.

"And at half-time, I told them that they [Slavia] are a team with huge spirit, they will keep running and keep believing. They will become more chaotic. We didn't control that at all, right from the beginning.

"We were on the back foot, very sloppy, we gave so many balls away, so many bad clearances. We didn't keep the ball in our structure at all. And then you have to suffer because teams in the Champions League are really good. A lot to learn."
Raya: Delighted with win but we can improve
Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya to TNT Sports:
"First half, we played really really well. We dominated the whole game, created a lot of chances and could have scored a few more goals.
"The second half was a completely different half. From them, they went up a gear.
"We were a little bit surprised and they made it really difficult for us - which we have to learn from.
"We know how important away games are and how difficult places like this can be. They became man-to-man all over the pitch.
"Delighted with the win, but we've got things to improve going forwards."
- Arsenal have won 13 matches in all competitions this season, the joint most of any side in Europe's big-five leagues along with Barcelona and Real Madrid.
- Nine of Noni Madueke's last 10 goals for Arsenal in all competitions have been scored away from home.
- Viktor Gyokeres has been involved in 16 goals in 25 Champions League appearances (12 goals, four assists).

articles.title: Billam-Smith vs Usyk? 'Maybe if he beats Benavidez and I beat Opetaia!'

paras.en: Chris Billam-Smith versus Oleksandr Usyk? 'Not next... Maybe if he beats David Benavidez and I beat Jai Opetaia!'

Oleksandr Usyk's potential return to cruiserweight would add a whole new dimension to the division; Chris Billam-Smith believes, with Usyk likely to fight David Benavidez, he can target Jai Opetaia once again; But Billam-Smith has a dangerous clash with Cheavon Clarke this Saturday first
Chris Billam-Smith could well benefit from Oleksandr Usyk’s plan to return to the cruiserweight division.
Usyk was an undisputed world champion at cruiserweight before he repeated that feat twice over at heavyweight, beating Tyson Fury, Anthony Joshua and Daniel Dubois among others.
But the great Ukrainian's team has revealed that he is now considering returning to cruiserweight before the end of his career.
It's a move the Billam-Smith, the former WBO cruiserweight world champion, welcomes.
"Probably it's fair to say it knocks me down a spot in the world rankings!" he told Sky Sports.
"But it's also great for the division, a huge name for the division that really probably has been the face of boxing, definitely in terms of achievement."
Usyk would be expected to target formidable cruiserweight champion David Benavidez, the current WBA and WBO titlist.

If Benavidez does box Usyk, it means he won't be fighting Jai Opetaia, another elite cruiserweight, next. Opetaia would still most likely return to cruiserweight after his December clash with Deontay Wilder but then he will be looking for an opponent himself.
That would be Billam-Smith's opportunity. He is still gunning for that fight.
"That definitely seems more doable now," he said. "I'm happy about that, because I think Benavidez would beat him and I always wanted to be the first man to beat Opetaia."

If Usyk wanted to re-accustom himself to boxing at cruiserweight before fighting Benavidez he could do worse than selecting a strong, come-forward, former world champion like Billam-Smith in an interim bout.
But Billam-Smith would expect Usyk to go straight into a fight with Benavidez, even though the Ukrainian hasn't fought since beating Rico Verhoeven in May.

"I think the level he's been and the level he's at in terms of marketable fights, I think he'd go straight into a Benavidez fight, especially at his age now," Billam-Smith said, before adding with a laugh: "I think taking interim fight, especially dangerous ones, against me, he doesn't need to be doing."

But Billam-Smith can dare to dream. On Saturday, live on Sky Sports, he fights Cheavon Clarke. Win that and it could be Opetaia next. Win that and he'd be right at the summit of the division. Then why couldn't an Usyk fight happen?
"Not next, maybe if he beats Benavidez, I beat Opetaia, that's a nice little southpaw to warm up with before I go in with Usyk," he said cheerfully.

Why is Usyk risking his legacy by making a potentially perilous return to the cruiserweight division? "Challenge. Purely challenge," Viddal Riley, the European cruiserweight champion, told Sky Sports.
"He keeps hearing: 'This guy's a monster, this guy's a monster' and then there's a part of him that just wants to show people: no, he's not a monster. I'm the guy. I've always been the guy.
"I think it's a lot of ego involved and it could backfire. It could backfire. People don't really go to heavyweight, come back down and look the same.
"I don't like to see the greats and the OGs do things like that because you're letting the goalposts move and trying to keep up when you've achieved everything you need to achieve.
"But it's still good for me and the division because we get spoken about more."
Watch Chris Billam-Smith vs Cheavon Clarke this Saturday live on Sky Sports.

articles.title: Norris unsure if Brazil upgrades will improve 'horrible' McLaren car

paras.en: Lando Norris: McLaren driver unsure if Sao Paulo Grand Prix upgrades will improve 'horrible' McLaren car

Reigning F1 world champion Lando Norris played down McLaren's upgrades which will be introduced at this weekend's race in Brazil; watch Friday's practice sessions for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from 3.30pm and 7pm, live on Sky Sports F1
Lando Norris is unsure if McLaren's upgrades at this weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix will improve the "horrible" handling on the car.
McLaren have not been in contention for victory in recent races, which Norris puts down to the team being outdeveloped by Mercedes, Red Bull and Ferrari.
With the aim of getting back to the front, McLaren have a new front wing, rear wing and floor components for Brazil as they look to hold onto third in the Constructors' Championship.

"They [the upgrades] are just to add performance," said Norris last weekend in Mexico.
"I don't think it will make it any easier [to drive]. Maybe there's a chance it makes it harder. For this you always leave it to the experts. I give my feedback, I say what I want, what's difficult.
"The engineers and aerodynamicists are the clever ones who turn my comments into lap time. They are doing a good job and continuing to work hard."
Norris won back-to-back races either side of the summer break in Budapest and Zandvoort, and should have won the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, if not for an unfortunate Virtual Safety Car.
McLaren introduced upgrades to the car in Baku in September and have not been at the sharp end of the grid since that event.
Norris, who is sixth in the F1 Drivers' Championship, says the car has "got better every time we brought upgrades" but is also unhappy with the MCL40's handling.
"The car has been horrible, difficult to drive the whole season. Just other teams have brought a lot more upgrades since and improved a lot more than what we have - nothing more than that," he said.

"The team are still doing a good job, considering we were 1.5 to one second off at the beginning of the year. The fact we won almost three races was a pretty sizeable achievement in itself, so we have had a pretty good year, if you want to look at it from that perspective.

"Of course we hold ourselves to a very high level and want to win everything we can. We started a long way behind at the beginning of the season and did a good job to catch up, better than the majority of any other team on the grid.
"Normally it's me looking at it from a negative way, but now I'm looking at it from a positive way. We want more, especially when we had a taste of success in the middle of the year."
McLaren have won the last two Constructors' Championships but are set to lose that mantle to Mercedes, who could secure that title this Sunday if they outscore Ferrari by at least three points.

Norris has been unable to put up a serious defence to his own drivers' crown and revealed McLaren may have suffered by putting more resource into last year's car, while other teams focused on the new 2026 regulations.

"I certainly wouldn't put this year at all in the direction of saying it's a failure. I think that's completely the wrong mindset to have, especially when we had to work so much on last year to win a world championship," he said.

"We knew we were going to pay the price, especially when you've got a bigger regulation change than ever in Formula 1. When you want to be able to drop everything and spend more time on something, it was a time we couldn't do that, because we had a Constructors and Drivers' Championship to win, so I'm more than happy that that was the sacrifice we took this year."

Norris suggested McLaren were disadvantaged earlier this year as they are a customer team to Mercedes and the complexity of the new power units meant the engine manufacturers benefitted the likes of Mercedes, Red Bull and Ferrari who all have their own power units.
"The first races were very tough. As a customer team to Mercedes, that obviously made things much tougher, so even if we had the same car, they would have beaten us," he said.

"You've got all these little things that add up to make it a tougher season than ideal. I think what made it tough was the fact we won races this season, which already I thought was a huge achievement in itself, to go from where we were at the beginning of the season to winning two, almost three races. I see that as a pretty huge success from where we were.
"What's hurt is the fact we've kind of drifted away from that, and more just other teams have brought big upgrades and improved in better ways than what we have over the last couple of months.

articles.title: Massive protests sweep Europe over cost of living and strained public services
articles.author: Freddie Clayton

paras.en: Massive protests were sweeping Europe on Saturday as part of demonstrations driven by the cost of living and deficient public services, with police bracing for potential violence after recent looting and riots.
Germany, France, Spain and Italy are among the nations where demonstrations were being held on Halloween following a recent wave of Gen Z-led marches across the continent.

French officials said they would deploy 70,000 police on Saturday following some of the worst rioting in decades, which erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education evolved into wider demonstrations about the cost of living and social security.
As the demonstrations began Saturday afternoon in Paris, protesters were pictured holding a banner that read: “We do not need tear gas for our future to be blurry.”
Videos vetted by NBC News show large crowds and fires burning in Marseille.

Some 320,000 people demonstrated across France on Saturday, including 70,000 in Paris, according to the French Interior Ministry. Authorities reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night.

While the protests have been largely peaceful, police arrested 1,300 people last week after an estimated 410,000 took to the streets in cities across the country. Stores, public buildings and businesses have also been damaged since the protests erupted last month.

“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said at a news conference earlier this week as he set out security arrangements, adding there was “a very high risk” of unrest.
Measures introduced last week to protect shops would be reinforced, he said, and demonstrations would not be permitted “in city centers, where there is a risk of public disorder.”
The U.S. Embassy in France advised travelers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.

The protests in France began after Prime Minister Emmanuel Macron launched budget talks for 2027. Students in the country, angry over a declining education system and the high cost of living, then took to the streets.
They were later joined by unions and the Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement that emerged in 2018 as a revolt against fuel taxes.
Those demonstrations appear to have inspired similar protests across the continent, with protests erupting in Belgium, Spain, Italy and elsewhere.
In Germany there were demonstrations organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt (Gen Z takes charge) in more than 30 cities Saturday, including the capital Berlin and the financial hub Frankfurt.
The groups demand spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and are against plans to return to mandatory military service.

“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Wiesbaden.
Protesters gathered in front of Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, as police said an additional 1,500 officers would be deployed throughout the city.
While most people rallied peacefully, some protests turned violent on Saturday night.

In downtown Frankfurt, some rioters smashed several storefronts and stole goods from inside. They also stole weapons from a gun store, which police were able to retrieve later. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.

Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.

In the United Kingdom, hundreds of demonstrators are expected to gather outside the U.S. Embassy in London on Saturday and risk arrest in support of Palestine Action, a protest group banned by the British government.
In Serbia, student-led activism also helped unseat the country’s long-time leader at the ballot box.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year after groups of masked protesters looted stores in the fashion capital and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police earlier this month.
Tens of thousands of people again took to the streets of Rome on Friday and other cities and towns across the country.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful, but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters.
Italian police were out in force with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the capital.

“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” said Luca, a 20-year-old medical student who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
CORRECTION (Nov. 2, 2026, 8:30 a.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated the capital of the German state of Hesse. It is Wiesbaden, not Frankfurt.

articles.title: U.S. military carries out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
articles.author: Gordon Lubold

paras.en: The U.S. military carried out limited strikes Monday on Iran’s Qeshm Island, according to two U.S. officials.

The officials said the U.S. attacks, which came on the eve of crucial U.S. midterm elections and as the Middle East is anxious about the possibility of a return to all-out war, were not a resumption of major combat operations in Iran. They described the attacks as self-defense in response to Iran’s ongoing efforts to target maritime shipping and U.S. assets.
The U.S. continues to intercept drones and missiles that are targeting shipping every day, one of the U.S. officials said.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has routinely targeted and shot at U.S. manned and unmanned aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz and in the area over the past few weeks, one of the U.S. officials said.
The U.S. is occasionally striking Iranian missile launchers in self-defense when the Revolutionary Guard shoots at U.S. aircraft, the official said.
Iran tried to target a U.S. aircraft again, leading to the U.S. strike on Qeshm to take out the launcher, the official said, calling it part of ongoing operations.
A third U.S. official said, “This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.”
Iranian state media reported that five explosions were heard Monday on Qeshm Island.
President Donald Trump had said the U.S. would not launch strikes on Iran before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Asked on “Fox & Friends” what would happen once the elections were over, Trump said he wasn’t looking to “kill lots of people,” but “if we have to, we’ll have to.” The latest strikes were “just a minor attack,” he said while insisting the situation does not constitute a war.
The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.

The administration was last known to have carried out some attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from getting to the global market. A third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal can still be struck to prevent Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, few details of which have been offered by the White House. Trump told reporters the letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.”
Vance suggested Monday that there was reason to believe the U.S. and Iran could still come to an agreement.

“We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” he told reporters when he was asked about the letter, adding that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.”

The region remains on edge about the prospect of the U.S.’ resuming full-scale operations against Iran. The back-channel efforts are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way forward in the eight-month-old war, which has rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed for renewed strikes even before the Israeli election last week as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.
But the war has also loomed large for American voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war appeared to show signs of progress.

Trump noted the drop Monday in a speech in Washington, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion.
“I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. Earlier he posted on Truth Social that “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible.”
He has frequently asserted that the two sides are close to a deal to end the conflict, though one has so far failed to materialize.
Iran has repeatedly said it is open to a diplomatic resolution but has largely stuck to its demands.

Tehran “has delivered a firm and rational response to the American side and the ball is now in America’s court to prevent a war,” Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tuesday.

articles.title: British backpacker sentenced for 'protracted' killing of dog in WA
articles.author: Nicholas R Ward, Jarrod Lucas, and Daniel Holmes

paras.en: British backpacker Bradley Gavin Knoesen, 31, has pleaded guilty to animal cruelty charges in Western Australia.
Knoesen, who is in Australia on a working holiday visa, drowned a kelpie before beating it to death.
Knoelsen has avoided an immediate jail term but is likely to be deported from Australia.
A 31-year-old British backpacker is likely to be deported after avoiding an immediate prison sentence over the "protracted" killing and "torture" of a pet kelpie in Western Australia's Goldfields.
This story contains graphic details some readers may find distressing.
Bradley Gavin Knoesen has been in custody in Kalgoorlie since the September 23 incident, which has been described as one of the worst animal cruelty cases seen in WA.
Described as a "dog lover" by his lawyer, Knoesen appeared in the Kalgoorlie Magistrate's Court on Thursday via videolink from Eastern Goldfields Regional Prison.
The court heard the 31-year-old had consumed an "extreme amount of alcohol" with his cousin when he picked up the one-year-old kelpie, named Faith, and repeatedly submerged her in water.
The dog lost consciousness and was briefly revived before being bludgeoned to death with a glass bottle by Knoesen, the court heard.
He then tied the kelpie to the back of his motorbike and dragged the body through bushland on the outskirts of Kalgoorlie.
Knoesen pleaded guilty to a charge of causing an animal unnecessary harm and received a suspended sentence of 12 months' imprisonment, which was suspended for 12 months.
The court heard Knoesen arrived in Australia in April on a working holiday visa and was employed in the mining industry as an underground truck driver when the incident occurred.
He had been living in Kalgoorlie with his aunt and cousin.
Defence lawyer Anthony Eyers said Knoesen was a "dog lover" and that his behaviour was "out of character" for the university graduate, who has a computer science degree.
Mr Eyres noted that Knoesen was likely to be deported from Australia.
Police prosecutor Amy Southall asked the court for an immediate prison term.
"It was absolutely gratuitous and unnecessary … shocking behaviour," she said.
The court had heard Knoesen repeatedly invited his cousin to join in and that the cousin asked him to stop and wept uncontrollably while the attack unfolded.
The prosecutor said that Knoessen told his cousin: "I want [the dog's owner] to see what happened to his precious dog."
Knoesen's connection to the dog owner, who was not his cousin, was unclear in court.
During sentencing Magistrate Donna Webb said the crime had outraged the public and was comparable to the worst cases of animal cruelty seen in the state.
She described the animal's death as a "protracted" act of cruelty.
"When I hear these facts, it strikes me more as torture … beyond comprehension," she said.
"His intoxication doesn't give any sort of explanation.
"Your client appeared to be incredibly determined to kill this animal."
Prosecutors argued for an immediate term of imprisonment, but Magistrate Webb gave Knoesen a 12-month suspended sentence, pointing to Supreme Court decisions in other animal cruelty cases.
The sentencing follows a separate case of animal cruelty last week in Perth, where a puppy farmer who kept more than 100 dogs in appalling conditions was sent to prison.
The case also comes just weeks after the RSPCA revealed animal cruelty reports from the Goldfields-Esperance region had jumped by 24 per cent last financial year to 256.
Most reports originated in the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which had 121, representing a 20 per cent increase on the previous year.
The RSPCA said 90 per cent of reports involved welfare concerns for dogs or puppies with insufficient care, inadequate food, water or shelter.
The RSPCA and the Department of Home Affairs have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Trust in the Reserve Bank is under strain, RBA deputy governor concedes
articles.author: Gareth Hutchens

paras.en: RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser says people are starting to lose faith in the RBA's ability to drag inflation down.
He says trust impacts inflation expectations of Australians.
The RBA's Monetary Policy Board lifted interest rates to 4.85 per cent this week, their highest level in 18 years.
Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser has acknowledged that Australians are losing confidence in the RBA's ability to bring inflation down as planned in the next 12 months.

He says a RBA survey has found that trust in the central bank's near-term ability to achieve its monetary policy objectives has "fallen materially" recently, even though overall trust in the RBA remains high and stable.
He says the RBA does not want the public to lose trust in the RBA as an institution, but economic developments are putting that trust "to the test".
"But inflation is another story. It's been above central bank targets for years.
"And around the world, that's causing increasing anger.
"Consumer confidence is exceptionally weak. And households rank inflation as their number one economic concern.
"The cumulative increase in prices since COVID has far exceeded that in any other tightening period since inflation targeting began.
"A lower inflation rate doesn't undo that accumulated increase. And it's that increase, not just the latest rate of change, that seems to be part of what's driving public anger.
"What impact has this had on public trust in central banks?" he asked.
Overall trust is high, but the edges are fraying

Mr Hauser made his prepared comments when delivering the Sir Leslie Melville Lecture at the Australian National University on Thursday evening. The title of his speech was Trust, Expectations and Monetary Policy.
In his lecture, he said the RBA had been running a new Community Research Survey, which began in February last year.
The survey has now had four separate waves, drawn on feedback from 12,000 Australians, across all parts of the country. The latest survey was in September.
He said the survey showed that around 55 per cent of respondents have 'high' or 'moderately high' trust in the RBA.
"That puts us in the upper part of the distribution of Australian public institutions," he said.
"Other central banks using comparable methodologies have similar scores.

"Strikingly, our overall trust measure has been broadly stable, or even slightly up, over the past 18 months. That's a welcome, but frankly quite surprising result over a period in which interest rates rose, and inflation rose well above the target range.
He said to answer that question, one has to look at how the more detailed survey responses have evolved.
And that's where one will find some worrying news.
"Unsurprisingly, trust in our near-term ability to achieve our objectives, looking one year back and one year forward, has fallen materially," he said.
"Regression analysis finds these outcome measures play a statistically significant role in explaining respondents' overall trust.
"Australians understand our inflation mandate and hold us accountable when we fail to meet it," he said.
In the graphic below, the final two blue rows show how Australians are losing faith in the RBA's ability to achieve its near-term inflation objectives.
Mr Hauser said trust played a very important role in the RBA's ability to manage Australians' inflation expectations.

But he said according to Macquarie University's Business Outlook Scenario Survey (BOSS), more businesses were becoming less sure that the RBA's inflation target will be achieved over the next 5-10 years.
"Some contacts in the RBA's liaison program say similar things," he said.
"Australia currently has no reliable measure of households' longer-term expectations, but their deep concern about inflation suggests they might feel somewhat similarly."
He said that was why the RBA was determined to do what it had to do to get inflation down.
Just as we need it most, trust is under strain
On Tuesday this week, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board lifted interest rates to 4.85 per cent, their highest level in 18 years.
Mr Hauser said it was imperative that the RBA maintained the trust of Australians in its ability to control inflation, especially now when the global economic situation was so fraught.

"The decades following the 1980s were good times for central banks around the globe, as flexible inflation targeting delivered consistently low and stable inflation alongside rising real incomes," he said.
"But more recently, and particularly since COVID, things have been rockier: persistent above-target inflation has marred that hard-won track record.
"The broader climate of trust towards public bodies has deteriorated.

"And we've entered a VUCA (Volatile, Uncertain, Complex and Ambiguous) world, amid a fusillade of shocks from tariffs, wars, geopolitical tensions, pandemics, and technological and environmental change.
"That means inflation is more likely to be pushed off target, economic forecasts are more likely to be wrong, and policy trade-offs get uglier.
"Just as we need it most, trust is under strain," he said.

articles.title: Six childcare centres to close in SA after failing to find buyer
articles.author: Madina Jaffari

paras.en: Six Edge Early Learning centres will provide their final day of care in Adelaide tomorrow, after administrators were unable to find a buyer for the sites.
The centres closing are at Mount Barker, Seacombe Heights, Flagstaff Hill, Port Augusta and two at Angle Vale.
Parents have been advised to contact nearby facilities to seek enrolment.
Six Edge Early Learning childcare centres will permanently close across South Australia on Friday after failing to secure a buyer, with families given as little as 48 hours' notice.
Edge Early Learning group tumbled into voluntary administration in August this year, with administrators KordaMentha securing buyers for many of the group's centres in SA and Queensland.

However, in a statement today, KordaMentha said they had "undertaken an extensive sale campaign", but had been unable to find a buyer for two centres at Angle Vale and one each at Flagstaff Hill, Mount Barker, Seacombe Heights and Port Augusta.
"Unfortunately, the campaign did not result in any acceptable offers capable of securing the ongoing operation of these services," the administrators said.
The latest announcement follows the closures of 11 other centres across Queensland, SA and the ACT last month.
Three of these centres were in South Australia, including Oaklands Park, Plympton and Royal Park.

KordaMentha said not-for-profit giant Goodstart Early Learning had been set to acquire the six centres as part of its initial proposal to buy 31 centres across Australia, but decided against it "during their due diligence work".

"After receiving this advice, the administrators liaised with the other purchasers of the Edge centre network, and other parties who had shown interest in these centres, but unfortunately have not been able to secure an alternative purchaser," the administrators said in the statement.
Families 'scramble' to find alternative care
Affected families were notified of the closures via a letter on Wednesday.
Parents at Edge Early Learning at Flagstaff Hill said they felt sad, frustrated and annoyed at the closures.
Rachael Brooks said she felt a "bit of panic" as she tried to find alternative care for her daughter.
"My daughter really loves it here, all the educators are really good people, I just feel so sad, so sad for them," she said.
"Obviously we've got work commitments and everything else, so a lot of pressure.
"Frantic kind of emails and phone calls, lots of message on the parent groups … feeling really sad and kind of worried about what's going to happen."
Vanessa Edwards said she felt "a little bit annoyed and a little bit frustrated".
"We were given such late notice and just left stranded without any other option,"
In the letter sent to affected families in Port Augusta, which the ABC has seen, families were urged to collect their belongings before the final day of care on Friday.
The letter also advised any fee payments made in advance would be refunded, and provided parents with details of an alternative option to enrol their children.
Andrew Padgett said he was shocked and frustrated the Port Augusta centre was closing.
"Shocked at first, then the realisation of how we're going to get care for our three-and-a-half year-old," Mr Padgett said.
"It's 48 hours' notice to get care for your child, it's a strange place to be, to try and scramble.
"If the writing was on the wall, why not tell us a couple months ago, and give us time to prepare.
"I think 48 hours not just for this centre but the other centres in South Australia is cruel, if anything."
Mr Padgett said it would be difficult for some families to find alternative care at short notice, and feared it could lead to families leaving the area.
"It's probably no shock to anyone that it is going to eventually lead to families having to leave Port Augusta and this community due to fact that there's no support," he said.
In the letter, families were advised to try Port Augusta Child Care Centre as an alternative.
However, Port Augusta City Council chief executive John Banks said the facility, which the council operated, was at capacity.
"Families interested in securing a place at the centre are encouraged to visit council's website and complete a waitlist application form," he said.
"Council is working to increase availability over the coming weeks."

Mr Banks said the council was notified of the closure this morning, and said it would have a significant impact on families, "particularly those who rely on accessible childcare to support their work and family commitments".

"Access to childcare is an important service for our community, and any reduction in available places can create additional pressure for families who may already be experiencing difficulty securing childcare," he said.
South Australia's Premier Premier Peter Malinauskas said he would seek more information about the closures from the federal government.

"Private childcare operators are 100 per cent the responsibility of the federal government and we are seeking urgent information from the federal government about what they're going to do to fix it," he said.

articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope plunges to Earth after 22 years in orbit

paras.en: NASA's Swift space telescope plunges to Earth after 22 years in orbit
Observatory's demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed
One of NASA's premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe's biggest explosions.
The Swift Observatory's demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed.
The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift's reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity in the past few years.
NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space's three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September.
- NASA telescope predicted to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
- NASA will no longer attempt to save its aging Swift space telescope
It was not immediately known how much of the nearly one and a half tonne spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated that some of the denser pieces would survive.

Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper.

Swift’s X-Ray Telescope captured the afterglow of gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A about an hour after it was first detected. The bright rings form as a result of X-rays scattered from otherwise unobservable dust layers within our galaxy that lie in the direction of the burst. (NASA/Swift/A. Beardmore, University of Leicester)

NASA is gauging industry interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses.

The space agency is looking for input from private companies about the possibility of boosting Hubble's orbit, upgrading its systems, guiding it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032.
Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, says Nicky Fox, NASA's science mission chief.

"Hubble still has important science ahead of it," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "And we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible.

articles.title: Valkyries celebrate WNBA championship with San Francisco and Oakland fans

paras.en: Valkyries celebrate WNBA championship with San Francisco and Oakland fans
The team honoured fans on both sides of the bay as they celebrated their victory Wednesday
The newest WNBA champs encouraged their California fans to call in sick, skip out on work or ditch school Wednesday — and elated basketball fans appeared thrilled to take their advice.
Tens of thousands of people lined the streets for a Golden State Valkyries victory parade after the team sealed the championship on Saturday in a 68-63 Game 7 win over the Atlanta Dream.

There was dancing, champagne, team colours and plenty of high-fives. And of course, team mascot Vi. She's a raven, commonly seen as a sidekick to Valkyries in Norse mythology, according to the team website.
Golden State Valkyries mascot Violet, also known as Vi, rides on a float during the team's WNBA championship parade. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)

The Valkyries began their day of celebration at Oakland's Jack London Square, not far from the team's downtown practice facility, then took a ferry across the bay to begin the parade from San Francisco's Ferry Building.
It concluded near the San Francisco Giants' Oracle Park.
Golden State Valkyries centre Kiah Stokes at the parade kickoff rally at Jack London Square in Oakland, Calif. (Yalonda M. James/San Francisco Chronicle/The Asscociated Press)
The players posed for photos onstage with the WNBA championship trophy at Jack London Square in Oakland before hopping on a ferry across San Francisco Bay. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Valkyries forward Kayla Thornton. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Golden State was granted an expansion franchise three years ago. At the time, team owner Joe Lacob guaranteed a championship within five years.

His promise was honoured as the team led by coach Natalie Nakase delivered an improbable title in Year 2 after becoming the first expansion franchise to reach the playoffs in its inaugural year in 2025.
Fans turned out for the parade in the team's colours from head to toe. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Valkyries fans cheered from a rooftop as the parade rolled past. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)
After the Dream beat the Valkyries in Game 3, Atlanta player Angel Reese taunted the Valkyries' bench with a hand gesture for "too small."
But some Valkyries turned the taunt into a power move after their victory, and brought it out for the parade.
Valkyries guard Juste Jocyte gives the 'too small' gesture, started by Angel Reese in Game 3, to the fans during the Valkyries parade. (David Gonzales/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Valkyries guard Tiffany Hayes celebrated from the double decker bus as it made its way through San Francisco. (Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters)

articles.title: Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in 2nd national security case

paras.en: Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in 2nd national security case
Wong is already serving a near 5-year prison term for his part in the city's biggest national security case

Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years in prison Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.

Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September he pleaded guilty to the offence, a move that can typically reduce the sentence.

The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city's biggest national security case after entering a guilty plea. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027.

Judge William Tam said during the sentencing hearing that Wong's offence was of a grave nature and rejected that his role was limited. He also said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea.
Wong looked calm and thanked his supporters before leaving the court. His supporters waved to him and Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism, once led by Wong, was in tears.
The judge said Wong could serve his two prison sentences concurrently. Wong only has about two months left on the sentence for his previous national security conviction.

Some members of the public started queuing outside the court building as early as Tuesday to secure a seat in the public gallery. Activist Lui Yuk-lin held a piece of paper carrying Wong's name in the line Thursday.

Resident ET Wong said that when Joshua Wong was just teenager, he possessed "big-picture thinking" that some adults might not even have. He walked a difficult path for Hong Kong's future, human rights and student movement, she said.
"At least in my heart, he should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment," she said.
People line up outside Hong Kong's High Court ahead of a Thursday morning sentencing. (Tyrone Siu/Reuters)

Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.
Observers say Wong's sentencing shows the authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism.

"NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law.
- Hong Kong's new security law expands scope abroad. What to know about the Article 23 laws
- Hong Kong activist Agnes Chow still fears Beijing's reach despite living in Canada

But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also said the security law is crucial for the city's stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.

Wong, second from left, with activists Eddie Chu, Owen Chow and Lester Shum, posing with signs in support of the 12 Hong Kong activists held in mainland China after attempting to flee the city for Taiwan, in Hong Kong, October 20, 2020. (Lam Yik/Reuters)
Prosecution focused on Wong's lobbying and advocacy

The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019.

After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries' attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.
His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.
His friends said during his nearly six years in prison, Wong has kept reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking.
To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.
Despite being held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp.

In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for "beautifying" his crimes. The city's security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.
But the documentary then shot to the top of Netflix's popular chart in Hong Kong.

articles.title: Indonesia deploys troops to Jakarta after wiretapping allegations

paras.en: Indonesia's military deployed more than 20,000 troops and personnel to the capital city, Jakarta, after authorities launched an investigation into an alleged wiretapping operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto.
Some 20,000 troops have been deployed in Jakarta amid a scandal with the president's chief of staff currently being investigated.
So far, three senior police generals have been detained. They are being accused of illegally tapping the phones of the president, journalists, politicians and business people.
Among those detained is Listyo Sigit Prabowo — not related to the president — who was the national police chief before becoming the president's chief of staff last month.
